100 EXPOSITIO. rum oculorum nutus, etc. Quae quidem omnia si re- ctè tractentur, iuxtaq́; literas, syllabas, dictiones, o- rationes, certo ordine, numeris adscriptis disposi- ta fuerint, admirandas facultates hominibus prae- stant, tantò excellentiores quantò quis peritior ac exercitatior fuerit in ijs disciplinis, quae circa princi- pia, causas, accidentia sensibilium versantur. Ta- lis est Catoptrice, quae docet visibilia rerum signa in momento referre visui, per certas imagines procul à nobis extra specula in aerem projectas, ad signifi- candam aliquam orationem institutas, quas facilè intelligit qui signum cognitionem habet. Caete- rum quo pacto fieri poßit, vt omnia ad signum v- sum transferantur, non est hujus instituti, sed ad Ste- ganographiam pertinet, cuius operis argumenta do- ctißimus vir Ioannes Trithemius in quadam epistola ad Bostium his verbis recenset, &amp;c. In manibus iam habeo grande opus, quod si vn- quam fuerit publicatum, quod absit, totus mundus mirabitur, cuius primi libri titulus est Steganogra- phia. Erunt autem quatuor libri, quilibet ad minus centum capitulis distinguetur. Incepi hoc opus ad in- stantiam vnius magni principis, quem nominare non opus est. quaeris quid hoc opus docet, omnibusq́; nescientibus stupenda incredibilia, quae à seculo nunquãm sunt audita. Primus enim liber continet plusquam centum modos occultè scriben- di, quicquid velis sine omni suspicione, sine literarum transpo- EXPOSITIO. 10I transpositione, sine omni timore, ita vt non fit homo in mundo, qui naturali industria scire, vel suspicari quidem poßit, quid in meis literis contineatur, prae- ter eum qui artem nouit ex me, vel ex eo quem ego docuero. Verba fun plana et familiaria, omni fu- spicione carentia, fed intentionem meam fine arte percipere poterit in aeternum, quantumcunque fit doctus, est res verè stupenda. Secundus liber multa mirabiliora continebit, per ignem videlicet in hac arte possum mentis mea conceptum fa- cere artem meam scienti ad quantamcunque distan- tiam,ad centum miliaria vel plura securè, fine ver- bis, sine scriptis, sine signis per quemcumque, nuncium, qui fi comprehensus in via fuerit, fi interrogatus e- tiam per tormenta durissima, nihil poteft fateri de nuncio meo, quia nihil fibi penitus constat de illo, quicquid occurrat, nuncium meum semper manebit occultum,nec omnes totius mundi homines fi fimul essent congregati possent illud vestigare virtute na- urali.Quod etiam facere fine nuncio dum volo pos- sum,voluntatem quoque meam indicare possum fe- lenti in carcere artem scienti etiam longè abfens quantumcunque custodiatur, etiam fi tribus milia- ibus sub terra federet. Et haec omnia latißimè et miuerfaliter quando quotiescunqe voluero pos- sum,naturaliter fine aliqua supersitione,vel adiu- orio spirituum quorumcunque.Mira fun fateor, ed audi mirabiliora.Tertius liber docet artem,per 102 EXPOSITIO. quam possum hominem idiotam scientem tantum linguam maternam, qui nunquam nouit verbum La- tini sermonis in duabus horis docere, scribere, legere intelligere Latinum satis ornatè disertè quan- tumque voluerit, ita vt quicunque viderint eius li- teras laudent verba, intelligant Latinè composita. Quartus liber continet multae stupenda experimen- ta, sed purè naturalia. Mentem videlicet me am in- dicare possum scienti artem meam inter edendum, vel seđendum cum alijs, sine verbis sine nutibus quam latißimè voluero, etiam inter loquendũ praedican- dum, ludendum in organo vel cantandum sine impe- dimento actionis alterius cuiuscunque, ita vt praedi- cando bona scienti clausis oculis, alia multa quartus liber continebit arcana quae non sunt in publicũ proferen- da. Mirantur haec omnes, qui audiunt, è quibus multi sunt viri nobiles atque, doctißimi, existimantes ista aut esse impoßibilia, aut penitus supernaturalia. His ego tibiꝙ; respondeo, quod multis respondi: multa natu- raliter esse poßibilia, quae nescientibus vires naturae impoßibilia, vel etiam supernaturalia videntur. Et ecce coram Deo meo loquor qui omnia nouit, quod ea quae praedixi miranda, quam ego scribere aut cre- dere poßis, tamen omnia sunt purè naturalia, sine deceptione aliqua, sine supersitione, sine magica ar- te, sine

Exposition.

[unclear] movements of the eyes, etc. All these things, if they are handled correctly and arranged according to letters, syllables, words, and speeches in a fixed order, with numbers assigned to them, furnish human beings with admirable powers, the more excellent in proportion as one is more skilled and practiced in those disciplines which deal with the principles, causes, and accidents of sensible things. Such is catoptrics, which teaches how to present visible signs of things to the sight in an instant, by means of certain images projected far from us outside mirrors into the air, devised to signify some speech; these are easily understood by one who has knowledge of the signs. But in what manner it can be brought about that all things are transferred to the use of signs is not the subject of this undertaking, but belongs to the Steganographia, the contents of which work the most learned man Johannes Trithemius sets out in a certain letter to Bostius in these words, etc.

I now have in hand a great work which, if it is ever published, which may it not be, the whole world will marvel at; the title of its first book is Steganographia. There will be four books, and each will be divided into at least one hundred chapters. I began this work at the urging of a certain great prince, whom there is no need to name. You ask what this work teaches: things astounding and incredible to all who do not know them, which have never been heard since the beginning of the world. For the first book contains more than one hundred methods of writing secretly whatever you wish, without any suspicion, without transposition of letters, without any fear, so that there is no man in the world who by natural skill could know, or even suspect, what is contained in my letters, except the one who knows the art from me, or from him whom I have taught. The words are plain and familiar, free from every suspicion; but [no one?] will ever be able to perceive my intention without the art, however learned he may be. It is a truly astonishing thing. The second book will contain many more wonderful things. By fire, namely, in this art I can make the conception of my mind known to one who knows my art at any distance whatever, at one hundred miles or more, safely, without words, without writings, without signs, through any messenger whatever. If he is seized on the road, if he is questioned even under the harshest tortures, he cannot confess anything about my message, because absolutely nothing is known to him about it. Whatever may happen, my message will always remain hidden, nor could all the men of the whole world, if they were gathered together, trace it out by natural power. I can also do this without a messenger whenever I wish. I can also make my will known to one who knows the art, even if he is silent in prison, though I am far absent, however closely he is guarded, even if he were sitting three thousand [miles?] under the earth. And all these things, most broadly and universally, whenever and as often as I wish, I can do naturally, without any superstition or aid of any spirits whatsoever. I admit they are wonderful, but hear things still more wonderful. The third book teaches an art by which I can teach an unlearned man who knows only his mother tongue, who has never known a word of the Latin language, in two hours to write, read, and understand Latin quite elegantly and eloquently, as much as he wishes, so that whoever sees his letters will praise the words and understand that they are composed in Latin. The fourth book contains many astonishing experiments, but purely natural ones. Namely, I can make my mind known to one who knows my art while eating or sitting with others, without words, without nods, as extensively as I wish, even while speaking, preaching, playing on the organ, or singing, without hindering any other action whatever, so that while preaching good things to one who knows, with eyes closed, [unclear]. The fourth book will contain many other secrets which are not to be brought out in public. All who hear these things marvel at them; among them are many noble and very learned men, who think that these things are either impossible or wholly supernatural. To them and to you I answer what I have answered many: that many things are possible naturally which, to those who do not know the powers of nature, seem impossible or even supernatural. And behold, I speak before my God, who knows all things, that those marvelous things which I have foretold, however much you may be able to write or believe, nevertheless are all purely natural, without any deception, without superstition, without magical art, without

Nam quod Albertum magno profundiimo rerum naturalium scrutatori comtigit, vt propter miranda quae occulta virtute natur ae operatus e, magus à vul go sit habitus, mihi sum certus militer contingere posse, si quaeris vnde mihi ia quae nemo nouit, audi. Non ab homine neque per hominem ia didi- ci, sed per reuelationem nescio cuius, cum enim prae- senti anno quadam vice cogitarem quid noui possem inuenire quod omnes lateret,coepi cogitare si ea pof- sem excogitare quaedixi miranda. Cum po longam phantasiam tanquam de re impoibili penitus de- sperarem,dormitumo,eonoe reposui,fatuitatem meam ipse mecum deridens quam impoibilia quae- rere tentauerim. Eadem nocte mihi atit quidam dicens,non funt vana ô Trithemi,quae nec tu nec alius tecum poteris inuenire,dixiq́;ad eum.Si ergo poibia sunt dic obsecro quomodo fiant.Et aperiens os uum,de singulis,per ordinem me docuit,oendens quomodo fieri,quae multis diebus frura cogitaueram,de facili poent.Ecce coram Deo quia non mentior sed veri- ratem dico,neminem ia adhuc docui,quamuis mul ti promittentes magna,saepe rogarint,praeter vnum principem cui scribo, quem de pofibilitate artis g 4 104 EXPOSITIO. manifesto argumento feci certiorem, nec decet ista alios scire, quàm principes, alioquin multa per ea fie- rent mala, traditiones, fornicationes &; alia quaecunque vellent homines mali. Sed benè v- tentes arte multa per eam reipublicae facere possent, possum autem ista omnia docere in omni lingua totius mundi quam audiui. Haec tibi Bosti propterea significare volui, ne me crede- res otiosum. Hactenus verba Trithemij. Postremo sunt aliae in- gentes vtilitates horum librorum Polygraphiae, quas in nostris libris de ratione docendi &; discendi tra- ctabimus, qualia cùnque enim haec videantur, tamen plus habent in recessu quàm in fronte promittunt. De Steganographia, cuius principia his libris ab- strusa latent, Deo volente, seorsim agemus. PRIMVS LIBER Polygraphiae. <Initial type="decorated-drop">Q</Initial>VATVOR sunt atque viginti si- gnorum sermonis Latini grammata, quae per ordinem praeposita totidem symanticis dictionibus, ad votum v- niuscuiusque operantis in hac arte copiosißimè per omnia deseruiunt arcanis. Sic autem para- EXPOSITIO. paraphrasmata sunt artificialiter ordinata, quod sermonem penitus Latinum efficiunt, si de quolibet ordine vna duntaxat capiatur. Et notandum quoda ratione sermonis nostri Theutonici, vicesima quarta littera w, in fine alphabeti assumitur, cum reliquae omnes vtriusque linguae ministerio perfungantur. Consignantes tali per ordinem industria locauimus, vt quamlibet de vnaquaque susceperis linea, summae deductione facta manebit concordia. Circumspectione tamen opus est, vt de qualibet syntaxeos linea non capias nisi vnam, & nullam monas binario facit iniuriã. Prouidendum quoque vt quotiens ad operazionem cabalisticam accedis, prius noctis minuta oꝫ singula numeres, eaꝙ; sequentis diei gradibus proportione debita coniungas. Quod si minutis arcano instituto diei gradibus finetenus non sufficiunt, cur sor ventosus ad archimensorem prudentẽ est confilio reducendus. Nec obstat si casu fortuito nox in caput diei recidat, cum prudens operator in arte tantundem per volũtariam appositionem à fron te poßit discedere, quanto noctem viderit diei lucem superare. Et hoc per totum Polygraphiae opus de singulis est capitulis intelligendum. Eam tamen considerationem vnitate dicimus, quabina-rius noto reuersionis indiculo, ne aberrare contingat, certificetur. Ex monade per constitutum binarius stabit, efficiturque, monas. Nihil hic frustra ponitur, nihil sine causa vel ociosum allegatur. Propterea mo g 5

Exposition.

[unclear], without the invocation or ministry of any spirits whatsoever. I have said this so that, if perhaps at some time a report should reach you that I can do wondrous things, you should not, I say, think me a magician, but a philosopher. For what happened to Albert the Great, that most profound investigator of natural things, namely that because of the marvels he performed by the hidden power of nature he was regarded by the common people as a magician, I am certain can happen similarly to me. If you ask whence I have these things, which no one knows, listen. I did not learn these things from a man nor through a man, but by the revelation of someone I do not know. For when, at a certain time in the present year, I was thinking what new thing I might be able to discover that would be hidden from everyone, I began to consider whether I could devise those wondrous things which I have mentioned. After a long imagining, when I despaired utterly of it as an impossible matter, I retired to sleep that night, laughing to myself at my own foolishness, that I had attempted to seek out such impossibilities. That same night someone stood by me, saying: “They are not vain, O Trithemius, the things which neither you nor another with you will be able to discover.” And I said to him: “If, then, they are possible, tell me, I beg you, how they are done.” And opening his mouth, he taught me each thing in order, showing how the things over which I had thought in vain for many days could easily be done. Behold, before God, I do not lie but speak the truth: I have so far taught these things to no one, although many, promising great things, have often asked me, except one prince to whom I write, whom by a clear proof I made more certain of the possibility of the art. Nor is it fitting that others know these things than princes; otherwise many evils would be done through them: betrayals, fornications, and whatever else evil men might wish. But those who use the art well could do many things through it for the commonwealth. Moreover, I can teach all these things in every language of the whole world that I have heard. I wished to make these things known to you, Bostius, for this reason: that you should not think me idle.

Thus far the words of Trithemius. Finally, there are other immense uses of these books of the Polygraphia, which we shall treat in our books on the method of teaching and learning; for whatever these things may seem to be, they nevertheless have more hidden within than they promise on the surface. On the Steganographia, whose principles lie concealed in these books, God willing, we shall treat separately.

The First Book of the Polygraphia.

There are twenty-four characters of the signs of the Latin language, which, set in order before the same number of significant words, serve most abundantly in all respects, according to the desire of each person working in this art, for secrets. But the paraphrases are so artfully ordered that they produce entirely Latin discourse, if only one is taken from any given order. And it should be noted that, by reason of our German language, the twenty-fourth letter, w, is taken at the end of the alphabet, while all the remaining letters perform the service of both languages. We have placed the signifying elements in order with such skill that, whichever you take from each line, once the deduction of the sum has been made, concord will remain. Yet care is needed, so that from any line of syntax you take only one, and the monad does no injury to the binary. One must also provide that, whenever you approach the cabalistic operation, you first count all the individual minutes of the night and join them in due proportion to the degrees of the following day. But if the minutes, according to the secret ordinance, do not suffice to the degrees of the day right to the end, the windy runner must by counsel be brought back to the prudent chief-measurer. Nor is it an obstacle if by chance night falls back upon the head of day, since a prudent practitioner in the art can, by voluntary addition, recede from the front by as much as he sees night exceed the light of day. And this is to be understood of the individual chapters throughout the whole work of the Polygraphia. Yet we call that consideration unity, by which the binary, by a known little sign of return, may be made certain, lest it happen to go astray. From the monad, through what has been established, the binary will stand, and it becomes a monad. Nothing is set down here in vain; nothing is adduced without cause or idly. Therefore

we necessarily warn that everyone who wishes to copy this work of ours, the Polygraphy, either in whole or in part, should diligently take care first of all not to depart in anything from our archetype, nor to skip, neglect, or transpose any word whatever. For indeed, if he has omitted one letter or word in essentials, if he has changed a word contrary to its nature, he has made the whole course of the work useless. Therefore let him either copy it properly, or not copy it.

The end.

Book I.

We rejoice that the end of the first book of our Polygraphy is at hand; made more ready for what remains, we judge that we must attempt what the powers of our talent may be. For newly invented things sometimes trouble the beginner, because he whom all follow has no one going before him. The first beginning of any invention is more difficult; after it has been made firm, it brings greater confidence to the author. Therefore, completing the first book of our invention with God’s favor and help, we have divided the whole into three hundred eighty-four small parts, placing beneath each, in order as is seen, the proper degrees of paraphrases. And these form a sufficiently beautiful Christian harmony, sixteen varied stations, with more than two hundred nine thousand phrases duly joined together in every respect. Nothing is lacking here for students of these inventions of ours, so that they may have the fullest knowledge and capacity in mystical, secret, and hidden matters, even those to be reported more remotely with the greatest safety. All things that are contained in the circle of art proceed from a point; their atoms constitute a circular line, and, by multitude of light, a straight one. Whatever

300 POLYGRAPHIAE quid extra lineam est, diei communi ratione deseruit, non nocti. Nox enim terminos mi- nutiarũ et paraphraseon semper inclusa nun quam egreditur. Quotiens igitur cum li neam rectam diei transieris, & nocturnae syn taxeos propositum non impleueris, caput retor queas ad caudam, & colligatione facta fiat li gamentum vtriufque ad inuicem. Vmbram sic ordina, vt solem non confundat similitudine vocis. Nec reuereare pudorem, si prima cal culatione dies non comprehenderit vmbram, sed linearum minutias connumera, donec pro portio necessaria ad votum subsequatur. Po teris etiam à primo saltum facere in secundũ, sciens quod in prima creatione dierum fa ctum est vespere et mane dies vnus. Propter ea vespere consummato, diem reduc in sequen tem, & signo dato per punctum binario simul et monadi notum fige mysterium. Verùm quo hanc euĩtare difficultatem poßis, orbis nostri totius, magnas revolutiones per gradus distin gue arithmeticos, & vbi dies pro nocte repe titur, notam Archimedis impone volanti, ne ternarius immaturus reditum ad unitatem bina- LIBER I. 301 binario intercludat. Nam propterea minu- tias singulis gradibus artificiosa inuentione praeposuimus, vt in his operantem à labore nu merandi paraphrasmata leuaremus. Si fue- ris industrius, diligens &; studiosus in his quae vt artis principia nouae tradidimus, crede no- bis maiora inuenies latentia quàm nos polli- citi sumus. Enimuerò cum in his naturalia plura contineantur arcana, vnum scias non vltimum, quod metatheseos operatione pru- denti, etiam cum voles peritißimum in hac arte facies ignarum, videntem coecum, &; do- ctum imperitum. Si falsa Hebraeorum esset vera opinio, orbium decem &; octo milium ho minibus singulis, ista adinuentio nostra singu- los daret modos tutè &; secretò scribendi ac nunciandi latißimè quaecunque Latinè vellent ar- canae. Of the Polygraphia ... whatever is outside the line, by the common reckoning of the day, has deserted the day, not the night. For the night, always enclosed within the limits of the minutiae and paraphrases, never goes beyond them. Therefore, whenever you have crossed the straight line of the day and have not fulfilled the purpose of the nocturnal syntax, turn the head back to the tail, and, a tying together having been made, let there be a bond of both with each other. Arrange the shadow so that it does not confuse the sun by similarity of sound. Nor be ashamed if, in the first calculation, the day has not comprehended the shadow; rather, count up the minutiae of the lines until the necessary proportion follows according to your wish. You will also be able to make a leap from the first into the second, knowing that in the first creation of days there was made evening and morning, one day. Therefore, when evening has been completed, bring the day back into the following one, and, when the sign has been given by a point known at once to the binary and the monad, fix the mystery. But so that you may be able to avoid this difficulty, divide the great revolutions of our whole sphere by arithmetical degrees, and where day is repeated in place of night, set the mark of Archimedes upon the flying one, lest an untimely ternary block the return to unity by means of the binary.

Book I.

For for this reason we have set minutiae before the several degrees by an artful invention, so that in these we might relieve the operator from the labor of counting the paraphrases. If you are industrious, diligent, and studious in those things which we have handed down as the principles of the new art, believe us, you will find greater things hidden than we have promised. Indeed, since many natural secrets are contained in these matters, know this one, not the least: that by the prudent operation of metathesis you will, even when you wish, make a man most expert in this art ignorant, the seeing blind, and the learned unskilled. If the false opinion of the Hebrews were true, this invention of ours would give to each man of eighteen thousand spheres his own methods for writing and reporting, safely, secretly, and very broadly, whatever hidden things he wished in Latin.

The second book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The reckoning-system of mortals tries, by art, to imitate nature, which admits no calculation of the monad. Hence, although the instruction of the preceding book of the Polygraphia, through the extension and metathesis of particulars, is as it were sufficient for the universals of this art in infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a certain consideration has moved us to join a second to the first. The condition of light is different in each; but night preserves inviolate, in both, the order of its course. The reader who is prudent, from small things and things not sufficiently brought to exactness, if he is strong in excellent natural talent, will be able to discover more polished things. Whatever visible thing is set in the whole circle of the universe gives ready support for the service of this new art of ours. Air and fire, water and earth,

Polygraphia, Book II.

earth, springs and rivers, trees, fruits, flowers, grasses, words, names, accident, substance, stones, sand, dung, filth, things, terms, honorable things, modest things, wood, metals, hard things, liquid things, existing things and non-existing things, history, fable, beasts, brute animals, human beings, draft animals, each and all things that either speech can express or the soul think, furnish the very broad field of our Polygraphia, and promise that the art, so far as it can stand for mortals, will have to be enlarged to infinity. For just as, from unity through the binary, the ternary generates the perfect number in the quaternary, so the consummation of this invention, standing through the quaternary in the binary as a twice-perfect root, gives us an infinite number beneath the minutiae of the things of the paraphrases of Polygraphia. For although among us all our things are terminable, nevertheless many things often occur which seem infinite to us because of the slowness of our understanding. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as a finite, circumscribable number can, by progression, be led into infinity, so the instruction of this art is enlarged by varied metathesis into immensity. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world is in every respect conformed to our instruction, nor is there anything known to us that is empty of mystery, if the method is understood by a master. But we, persuaded by reason, stand under the service of the binary and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is there given an occasion by which we might raise our attempt to weightier matters; if it should be offered to us acceptably, we shall not refuse to make more important things manifest to those who desire them.

For it is written: Where there is no hearing, never pour forth speech. Therefore, adding a second book to the first of the Polygraphy, we keep its form and method, setting in the light of day three hundred and eight paraphrases in simple progression, for the honorable remembrance of the most chaste Mother of God; if a suitable time had been available, [unclear] to give more elegant things, so that it might both add brilliance to the matter and sufficient progression to the form. The first inventor of any art transmits greater things to posterity, because, since the beginnings of an art are hard and unfamiliar, no subtle invention is found complete from its origin. From [Peapoli?], which is also Herbipolis, a city of the Eastern Franks, on the twelfth day of the month of February. In the year of the Lord 1508.

With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, who lives in the sacred ternary unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, threefold in persons and one God in substance, incomprehensible, omnipotent, and everlasting, from whom, in whom, and through whom proceeds every good, beautiful, and true thing, we have brought this second book of the Polygraphy to its end. To him be praise, honor, virtue, and glory: he who, through the innocence of his death, freed our race from the destruction of eternal perdition, and, with perpetual mercy, opened again the entrance to eternal life for all who believe in him with a pure conscience. Line by line we have set down three hundred and eight paraphrases, deliberately avoiding a longer wandering [unclear]. For it seemed enough to us at the beginning of this lucubration if we gave those wishing for larger matters a reason to seek them out, since both time and method for these things were lacking to us. Farewell, friendly reader. From Peapolis, on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508. IOAN-

The third book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

What, from the beginning of human creation, confused the unity of language? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing outward those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself. Yet of this ministry of the mind’s secrets to the senses there are many modes, whose properties vary both by use and by art. Use, introduced at pleasure, is common to many; art, however, to few. Indeed no one will readily estimate how much the very unregulated use of speaking among the Germans alone has varied in six hundred years, who has not rather often reread Otfrid, monk of Weissenburg, in the poems of the German tongue. The sea flows and ebbs; men, once dying, do not return again to the present life. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines with respect to better things.

Who today among the Germans, ancient emulators of the Greeks, possesses the old knowledge of idioms? In the chronicles, the ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibaldus, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed many things said in old verse, in the prose of the German speech, into their compositions, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, Thuringians, daily undergoes notable variation? Men are changed in time, customs vary, minds are changed, clothes vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient property of idioms is varied; nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a vicissitude of all things; variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to reduce this perpetual flowing away, so to speak, to the concord of unity?

But the fact that we add a third to the preceding books of the Polygraphy has not lacked a special reason. For, since the wills of men are various, rightly there are given manifold modes for honorable operations. In those, day illuminates night; in these, however, day lacks light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, the blind illuminates the blind, and, existing and remaining sight without eyes, ministers in darkness what it does not have. Here night darkens day with perpetual gloom, and one walking in darkness without light provides blind guidance. These paraphrasms serve all men throughout the world, and in every language transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latinity moves barbarians to laughter, and barbarism itself produces suspicion among Latin-speakers. Yet it matters nothing or little, since however great suspicion may have been, it will nevertheless contain every most secret mystery. Let the diligent operator recall to mind the rules and precepts which we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed; without it the usefulness of no art will stand. Thus in a few things we have shown the way to the greatest matters, and, with a finite mode, we have given the way to infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared for friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde mark can be fixed in every place until you take up the mark of rest. Farewell. From Peapoli, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

V pasur V gomut V vadui 1052 X pasai X gomei X vadal 1053 Y pasei Y gomij Z vadil 1054 Z pasij Z gomoi w vadol 1055 w pasoi w qvod MAOI VOD in principio tertij Polygraphiae nostri operis sumus polliciti ad habendam glossae no- quae vmbram similitudinem coram inex- pertis, laboris compendio satis fecimus ad exemplum. Noctem arcanis tuto seruientè, vmbris periphrasma- tum ducēdam commissimus, numeros ordine qua- tuor linearum telotenus interposuimus pro vsu vo- lentium adaptatos. Loca sunt minutiarum gradus habẽtia fixos tria milia centũ quinquaginta, quam- quam horarum restent momenta si volueris infi- nita, pro secretandis in omni natione lingua orbis quicquid arcani occurrerit. Orbem linealiter na- scentem ex puncto, quantum volueris, opus fuerit, reducere po- teris ad semitam qua venisti. Si noctis superest mul- tum, reducito caudam draconis ad caudalitium ori- ginale in caput. Verùm binarius omnino fit certifi- catus de notis signaculis vnitatis. Qui multum e- furit, multum laboret, vt habeat quod manducet. Nec est opus magni laboris id quoꝛ sum volueris duce- re, quod sua sponte progreditur. Hic ergo finem ter- tio Polygraphiae nostrae libro constituimus, in nomine Patris Filij Spiritus Sancti. Lector mitis vale. Ex Peapoli 7. die mensis Martÿ, Anno Do- mini Iesu Christi saluatoris no- stri 1508. Indictione vndecima. IOAN- 508 IOANNIS TRI- THEMII ABBATIS MONASTERII S.IACO- BI MAIORIS POSTOLI VVIRCI- burgensis, quondam Spanheimensis, Or- dinis Diui Benedicti, quartus Polygraphiae Liber incipit. <Initial type="decorated-drop">C</Initial>RDO expostulabat ra- tionis quartum Polygra phiae nostrum librum, qualitate, inuentione facili- tate dissimilem fie- ri praecedentibus: quate- nus volentes rerum partici- pari arcanis non vno sed varijs id modis assequantur atque diuersis. Extendimus picam facilima inuentione comprehen- sibilem, vt nox per minutiã semper con- cta monadi quolibet ordine in lumine cognoscatur diei. Nulla isthic inter vni- tatem binarium reperitur dissensio: neque oportebit artis instrumentum o- perari volentẽ habere ad manum, quan- do pri-

What, at the beginning of the third book of our work, the Polygraphia, we promised, namely to provide for the sake of the semblance of a [unclear] gloss before the inexperienced, we have fulfilled sufficiently, by a concise labor, as an example. We have entrusted the night, safely serving hidden things, to be guided by the shadows of periphrases; we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines all the way to the end, adapted for the use of those who wish to employ them. The places of minutes, having fixed degrees, are three thousand one hundred and fifty, although, if you wish, infinite moments of hours remain for concealing, in every language of every nation of the world, whatever secret matter may arise. The circle, arising linearly from a point, as far as you wish and as the work requires, you will be able to lead back to the path by which you came. If much of the night remains, lead back the dragon's tail to the original tail-place at the head. But the binary is made altogether certain from the known signs of unity. Let him who rages greatly labor greatly, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is there need of great labor to lead wherever you wish that which proceeds of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set an end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell.

From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh indiction.

508 The Fourth Book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James the Greater, apostle, at Wuerzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The order of reasoning demanded that our fourth book of the Polygraphia be made unlike the preceding ones in quality, invention, and facility, so that those wishing to share in secret matters may attain this not by one method but by various and different ones. We have extended a system easily comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that the night, always connected through the minute to the monad in whatever order, may be recognized in the light of day. Here there is found no disagreement between unity and the binary; nor will it be necessary for the person wishing to operate the instrument of the art to have it at hand, when pri-

98
do primae succedens fine medio, latens ostendit mysterium. Vnde prudens, intelligẽs, &; expertus scientiam, omni tem pore &; loco, fatisfaciet operationi. Binarius ab vnitate recipit, vnde terna- rium producit. Facilis est huius crypto- logiae facie prima cognitio: posteaquam luna vel puncto vnico fuerit à sole illu- strata. Quamuis &; fieri possit, quòd gno sticus euadat industrius sine manudu- ctione magistri. Quod in isto tamen li- bro tantùm reor intelligendum, in prae- cedentium verò nullo. De sequentibus autem suo dabitur loco iudicium. Inter omnes quos dedimus praesentiatus cabalisticus arcanorum modus, istius li- bri quarti progressus facilior in infini- tum potest extendi. Quare sufficit me cupientibus ampliora formam tradidis- se simul &; causam exempli. Lumen in- telligentiae haec facilè penetrat omnia. Scripsi Peapolis, nona die Martij, Anno Domini millesimo quingen- tesimo octauo. [unclear], succeeding the first with the middle as end, reveals the hidden mystery. Hence the prudent man, understanding and experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary receives from unity, whence it produces the ternary. Knowledge of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun with even a single point. Although it can also happen that the knower becomes skilled without the guidance of a teacher. Yet I think this is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning those that follow, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic modes of secrets that we have presented, the progression of this fourth book, easier than the rest, can be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the cause of the example. The light of understanding easily penetrates all these things. Written at Peapoli, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Demonstratione poßibilitatis nouae adinuen- tionis nostra, quam breuiter nec minus suffi- cienter ostensa, non arbitror me ipsum in eadem hac vice diutius fatigandum cum iter modus praestet in infinitum, si cui ad vlteriora fuerit exemplar necessa rium. Minimè quoque reor necessarium ea quae sunt recitata in praecedentib.ad memoriam reducere,cum Lector sagax si fuerit studiosus etiam quae in his ma- iora latitant poßit auxiliante domino inuenire.Ma- teriam sapienti et studioso tradidimus simul et cau sam,quibus si prudenter vti voluerit, sue nostrum in- genio superabit.Quisquis verò hanc statam cupit in vmbra pulchriorẽ, ingenio manum coniungat et ani mũ,& iter sibi faciat ipse paraphrasmate pulchrius decoratum.Memoria teneat fixum si quem ista dele- ctãt vt in orbe semper maneat praestituto, quem quo- libet modo praetergressus fuerit,operatio tota inutilis euanescit.Hominum plura nomina, sunt denique infinita penè vocabula rerum,villarum,lapidum et ver- borũ,quae nostris omnia subseruiunt institutis.Ex hiis librum et modum fieri cõstat non impoßibile, si cum diligentia fit praesto ingeniũ, quae nostra inuenta prae- cellant in infinitum.Qui verò tantae fuerit hebetudi- nis vt haec puerilia nostra intelligere nequeat,eacuae subtiliora restabunt quando penetrabit? Finem li- bro Polygraphiae quarto imponimus,cui quintum in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi sociamus. IOAN- 551 IOANNIS TRI- THEMII ABBATIS SANCTI IACOBI APOLITANI Polygraphiae liber quintus exordium capit. <Initial type="decorated-drop">E</Initial>A quae auxiliante Domino nostro Jesu Christo in quatuor praecedentibus libris pro comple- mento Polygraphiae nostrę vtcunque digessimus, rationabiliter exigunt, vt reliqua huiuf- ce institutionis praecepta quae superfunt modos, breuiter in quinto pertractemus. Dabimus itaque modum in eo fatis compendiosum per metathefin, id eft, transpositionem literarum, quo fecurè, tuto, secretiffimè amicus scribet ad a- micum quaecunque voluerit. Eo scribendi modo Caefarem Auguftũ legimus vfum in arcanis. Qui quidem nunciandi mo- dus etfi multipliciter fit fecurus, femper tamen 552 POLYGRAPHIAE tamen intuentibus habetur suspectus: quia mox vt literarum cernitur transpo- fitio, qui curlofus eft aliquid fubcis late re protinus fuspicatur. Sunt autem modi huius adinuationis penè infiniti, è quibus nos pro neceffaria introductio-ne fequentes lectori praesignauimus, cu-ius reliqua ingenio perscrutanda refer-uamus. In primis ergo tabulã huius industriae praefissimus canonicam, cui alte ram subiecimus auersam. In his duabus tabulis radix et fundamentum memora-tae trãspositionis omnino ponitur, super quo structura totius aedificij collocatur. His etenim duabus tabulis ritè cognitis et intellectis, nulla trãspositio literarum latere poterit, cum diligentia operãtem. His quatuor et viginti alphabeta per ordinem coniunximus, vt lectori copiam transponendi grammata praeberemus. Horum vsus provoto cófitit in fingulis, aut fi malueris etiam in vniuerfis. Si tibi cum multis fuerit arcani commercium, alphabeta fingula familiaribus tuis diftri bue fingulis, tu verò memoriae commenda quid M LIBER V. da quid vnicuique tradideris. Primo qui- dem alphabetum committatur primũ, secundo secundum, tertio tertium, & ita consequenter fiat de reliquis. Quod si prae multitudine negociorum aut fami- liae alphabeta quae signauimus non suffi- cerẽt ad omnia, vel si aliqua ex eis nimis videantur patula manifesta, varias trãs positiones nouas poterimus inducere, quarum numerus perpetuo maneat semper oc cultus. Cuius rei ponamus exemplum: B fit a, f fit b, p fit c, t fit d,z fit f,c fit g,m fit h, ita consequenter per totum alphabetum vsuale fiat vt inter quamli- bet literam assumptam tres interiaceant ociosae ac transpositae. Postea quatuor, deinde quinque, plures aut pauciores,i- ta tamen quod totum alphabetum qua si reuolutum in orbem concurrat, sed vnaquae que eadem serie pro alia in ordine suo collocetur. Qualicunque modo scripseris ipsum aut memoriae tenaciter noueris cõmendandum, ne per obliuio- M5 nem

With the possibility of our new invention demonstrated, which has been shown briefly and no less sufficiently, I do not think that on this occasion I myself should be wearied any longer in the same matter, since the method offers a path to infinity, if anyone should need an example for further matters. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been recited in the preceding books, since a discerning reader, if he is studious, can, with the Lord’s help, discover even the greater things that lie hidden in these. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the reason; if he wishes to use them prudently, he will surpass our work by his own talent. But whoever desires this [unclear] to be more beautiful in the shade, let him join hand and mind to talent, and let him make a path for himself, more beautifully adorned with paraphrase. Let anyone whom these things delight keep fixed in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men, and finally there are almost infinite terms for things, villages, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that a book and a method can be made, not impossible, if talent is at hand with diligence, which may surpass our inventions without limit. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the more subtle matters that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we join the fifth.

The fifth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, begins.

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have arranged as best we could in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphy, reasonably require that in the fifth book we briefly discuss the remaining precepts of this instruction, the methods that still remain. Therefore in it we shall give a sufficiently compendious method by metathesis, that is, the transposition of letters, by which a friend may securely, safely, and most secretly write to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used that method of writing in secret matters. Although this method of sending messages is in many ways secure, nevertheless to observers it is always regarded with suspicion, because as soon as the transposition of letters is seen, anyone who is curious at once suspects that something lies hidden beneath. Now the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from these, for a necessary introduction, we have marked out the following for the reader, reserving the rest to be investigated by his talent. First, therefore, we have placed at the head a canonical table of this practice, beneath which we have set another, reversed. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforementioned transposition is entirely placed, upon which the structure of the whole building is set. For when these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to escape one who works diligently. To these we have joined twenty-four alphabets in order, so that we might give the reader abundant means of transposing letters. The use of these consists, according to one’s wish, in each individually, or, if you prefer, also in all together. If you have secret correspondence with many people, distribute the individual alphabets to your individual acquaintances, but commit to memory what you have handed to each one. To the first, indeed, let the first alphabet be entrusted, to the second the second, to the third the third, and so let it be done in sequence with the rest. But if, because of a multitude of business or of household members, the alphabets which we have marked should not suffice for everything, or if some of them seem too open and evident, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, the number of which may always remain perpetually hidden. Let us set down an example of this matter: let b be a, let f be b, let p be c, let t be d, let z be f, let c be g, let m be h; so consequently through the whole usual alphabet let it be arranged that between any letter assumed and its substitute three idle and transposed letters lie between. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, in such a way, however, that the whole alphabet, as if revolved into a circle, meets together, but each letter is placed for another in its own order in the same series. In whatever way you write it, you must know that it is to be firmly entrusted to memory, lest through forgetfulness

Tot enim modis litera- rum transpositio potest, quot se- cundum aestimationem intellectus hu- mani qui operatione temporali conclu- sus in corpore mortali nō capit proprie infinita, mortalis cõfurget numerus in- numerabilis. Vnde quicunque modos scribendi per metathesin et plures habe- re voluerit et à nostra institutione remo tos, si vel parum fuerit ingeniosus et di- ligens, facilem in operatione sua confe- quetur effectum. Maxima enim potest ingenium hominis si studio iuuetur et arte. Qui autem spernit minima, nun- quam pertinget ad maiora. Scio pleros- que futuros qui haec studia nostra in va- na et puerilia deridebunt, quibus damus pro responso, nos omnino fore conten- tos modò illis complaceant, ad quo. composita. 554. Polygraphy, Book V.

…[such] a lapse that you yourself can no longer read what you had written. For the transposition of letters is possible in as many ways as—according to the estimation of the human intellect, which, enclosed in a mortal body by temporal operation, does not properly grasp the infinite—a mortal but innumerable number rises up. Whence whoever shall wish to have more modes of writing by metathesis, and ones remote from our system, if he be but a little ingenious and diligent, will easily achieve the effect in his own working. For the talent of man can [accomplish] the greatest things, if it be aided by study and art. But he who spurns the least things will never attain to the greater. I know there will be very many who will deride these our studies as vain and childish; to whom we give for answer that we shall be entirely content, provided they please those for whom they were composed.

There follows the Straight Table.

555. The Straight Table of Transposition.

[transposition grid, as printed]

In this canonical or straight table of letters you have, from our one and usual [alphabet] of Latin letters themselves, by their permutation or transposition, as many alphabets as there are monograms throughout it—namely four-and-twenty times twenty-four, which make in number 576; and multiplied by as many again, they yield a little less than fourteen thousand.

556. The Reverse Table of Transposition.

[reverse transposition grid, as printed]

In this reverse table you have, by the transposition of letters, as many alphabets as we marked in the preceding straight [table]. For, as you see, under the metathesis there are 24 to the right; to the left likewise as many; downward 23; and upward 23. Which, multiplied 24 times by 93, reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, make alphabets not fewer than 112.

There follows the same table expanded.

557. The First Figure of the Expansion of the Straight Table.

[expansion grid, as printed]

This is the first figure of the expansion of the straight table, having five alphabets by metathesis, with the letters transposed as is seen. For in the first alphabet, for a is taken b, for b is taken e, and so on consequently, as appears more clearly to one looking. In the second alphabet, for a let c be taken. In the third, d; in the fourth, e—as the placement of the order teaches.

Let the expansion be continued.

563. The Second Figure of the Expansion of the Straight Table.

[expansion grid of letter-pairs, as printed]

In this second figure of the expansion of the reverse table the alphabets are six in number, in the first of which k, in the third i, in the fifth h, are not changed. And since the norm has so given it, it makes no difference; for in so great a multitude of variety no one, even the most expert, will be able to weigh out the constancy of a single mark or character.

Continuation of the table. [N 2]

564. The Third Figure of the Expansion of the Reverse Table.

[expansion grid, as printed]

In this third figure of the expansion of the reverse table there is nothing new of its kind except the metathesis, which is common to all in degrees almost infinite. Six alphabets are transposed. In the first t is eclipsed, in the same g, in the third s, and c, r, and e—the cause of which thing the norm teaches.

Continuation of the table.

565. The Fourth Figure of the Expansion of the Reverse Table.

[expansion grid, as printed]

In this fourth figure of the expansion of the table several errors of the defect of letters concur according to the canonical reckoning; which, since they can easily be emended, I did not wish to depart from the norm of the system. In the first q and d, in the fifth c, in the fifth also b, are not changed.

Continuation of the table.

566. The Fifth Figure of the Expansion of the Reverse Table.

[expansion grid, as printed]

In this fifth figure of the expansion of the reverse table there are only two alphabets—the first in order—looking upon it[self], in the number of which a is eclipsed in the first. But the remaining four [are left] for forging new ones at will.

Hebraei quarundam duplicate li- terarum notas octo et viginti ad omnem numerum sufficientes instituerũt. Graeci verò hunc literarum defectum quatuor appositione characterũ simili prouiden- tia subleuarunt. Nos ergo v̄ literas qua- tuor habentes et viginti, quare et nostras nõ facimus numerales, qui similiter qua- tuor possumus inuenire duplicatas? De- mus quatuor in exemplum, & satis om- nem erit ad numerũ, m et iij. finale. item r et 2 finale. item s longum et s finale siue clausum. item v clausum et u apertum. His dum xxiiij. literas vsuales adiũgimus, octo et viginti numeris sufficientes om- nibus 573 nibus characteres habemus.Eritq́; haud magni laboris negocium hūc numeran- di apprehendere modum, his qui literas iam nouerunt, si eum semel memoriae commendauerint.Poterit enim haec no- stra inuentio multis multa milia compre- hendit in numero, quę omnia primo in- tuitu sine calculatione aliqua luce cla- rius discerni possunt et intelligi. Quod fieri per figuras algaritmi praesertim in numeris magnis tā facilè non posse mul tis videtur, minus in arte calculatoria ex- pertis. Mox enim vt oculo numerum quantumlibet magnum inspexeris eum et plene intelligere, & exprimere poteris sine circumlocutione seu diuisione ser- monis. Quod quam sit facilè conueni- ens est vt literas ipsas in numerum redactas consignemus. Scri- psi 16. Martij. Anno 1508. Ordo

In the present Orchema a manifold alphabet is handed down by transposition and leap, both by the rule of order and by the position of the letters. All these things suffice as an example for those who cannot be content with the arrangements already given, so that they may have a method and form for discovering the remaining ones, since they can be varied without number, as the following expansion of the Orchema clearly teaches.

Johannes Trithemius [Peapolitanus?] to the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the painstaking Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve for the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews established twenty-eight signs of certain duplicated letters, sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, with like foresight remedied this deficiency of letters by the addition of four characters. We, therefore, having twenty-four letters, why do we not make ours numerical too, since we can likewise find four duplicated ones? Let us give four as an example, and that will be sufficient for every number: m and final iij; likewise r and final 2; likewise long s and final, or closed, s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-four letters in common use, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers.

And it will be no very laborious matter to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know the letters, if they once commit it to memory. For this invention of ours will be able to comprise many thousands upon thousands in number, all of which can be distinguished and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. Many, less experienced in the art of reckoning, think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of the algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have inspected with your eye a number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is so easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number.

I wrote this on 16 March, in the year 1508.

Behold, reader, you have the method by which every number capable of being written can sufficiently be marked and written with a few letters; their extension, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But, as it was once customary to say in a proverb, “the weary ox plants his foot firmly”: whoever wishes to be content with former things should follow the ancient method of numbering. So that those who do not know it may understand it more easily, it will not be tedious for me to give, in what follows, the form which Hunibald, historian of the Franks, and also Bede, Rabanus, the monks Helpericus, and several of the ancients used in chronicles and ecclesiastical calculations, as follows.

Humano post haec multiplicato genere, in omnem terram vbique, diffuso, non diu mansit vni- tas literarum, sed corporum animorum proculab inuicem diuisio, diuerfos varios inuenit modos scri-bendi, de quibus longa nobis narratio. 578

Here begins the sixth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg.

Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still rude in intellect and uncultivated in morals, under the rule, shared by alternation, of three intelligences, as certain persons think, succeeding one another in order through one thousand sixty-three years, the influences of the planets in the sphere are said to have presided in their own way over bodies on earth by their influence, chiefly under the governance of their intelligence, whom they called Orisiel, that is, the life-giver of God, for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and as many days and hours. These things we recount as poetic, not as affirming them.

After Saturn, Venus is set down as having assumed dominion; after Venus, Jupiter. But after Jupiter, Mercury, the fourth ruler in order, adorned human talents with various arts. Under the three intelligences already mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence, whenever one person wished to announce something secret to another, he did it not by writings, since the function of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees, plants, or of some other sensible things, just as they had agreed among themselves.

The time of Saturn, as they say, gave to human beings morals properly suited to his influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, woodland-dwelling, gloomy, simple, uncultivated in life and morals, living for a long time in the flesh. After Orisiel of Saturn, as those who hold this opinion say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, receiving the government of the world by influence, continued it for three hundred fifty-four years, and for four months, days, and hours; under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses and cities more frequently, and also to discover various manual arts, namely weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to flow away much more into pleasures of the flesh, and to take beautiful wives, and, many children having been begotten by them from these wives, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the cithara, and more eagerly devised whatever they affirm to pertain to the influence of Venus, following the motion of the flesh.

They named the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel; when it received dominion of the world after Anael, it made human beings restless with desire for ruling, to carry on hunts, to make tents, and to adorn themselves with various garments. While he was ruling, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, a great division arose between the good and the bad: the former calling upon God, but the latter given over to the flesh and to the world. Under his rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

But the fourth mover or angel of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year of the world at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. But the letters then, as they report, were very different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time afterward these were changed in many ways, and took on an easier manner of formation and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding deity of all literature, promising that great secrets of things lay hidden beneath fables. After this, when the human race had multiplied and had been spread everywhere over all the earth, the unity of letters did not remain long; rather, the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered different and various modes of writing, about which our narration is long. Plato the Philosopher

[unclear] in the Phaedrus relates that letters and the use of writing, together with the system of weights and the game of dice, were first invented by a certain philosopher named Theuth, and that he taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost every nation and people, letters that remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose to set down or describe the account. For all the more learned men among us know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α, ε, γ, δ, ζ, ω, λ, μ, ν, ι, θ, ξ, π, σ, τ, ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: ξ, θ, φ, χ. And Pythagoras afterward added the letter u, so that there would be twenty in all; ζ, κ, ω were subsequently invented by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters of their own. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters too was varied in many ways. Hence it came about that the use of letters in the course of time arrogated to itself such license that not only individual peoples, but also particular men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding-places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unfamiliar character will not be free from suspicion among those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a private mode of writing, separate from the common one, caring little for the suspicion of others, provided that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. Moved by imitation of these, and desiring to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as possible, to a finished end, in this sixth book, which is also the last, I have resolved to recall from the dead certain characters of the ancients, which long ago passed out of human use, lest they perish entirely; and first indeed we shall set down the ancient mode of writing of the Nortmanni.

On the Alphabet and Wonderful Mode of Writing of the Nortmanni, at the Time When They Were Ravaging [unclear].

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said before, whereas of the Latin letters, which we Germans also use, only seven are counted as numerals, namely c, d, i, l, m, y, and x. The Nortmanni, however, together with the Asiatic Dacians, having gone out from the Scandian islands, which are now called Gothic, overran Gaul for more than forty years and laid it waste most grievously. In order to provide for their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk bears witness, they devised a new and elegant mode of writing from the letters of the Greeks, as follows. For they adapted the numerical values of the Greeks, comprised in ten of their twenty-four letters, to Latin characters, and under a foreign appearance prudently concealed our letters, in precisely the way in which we use numbers in place of letters, that is, when for a we put 1, for b 2, for c 3, for d 4, and so on in succession to the end of the alphabet. It is indeed a fine and quite secure invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six; and in this mode of writing, representing f, the sixth letter of the Latins, and, in addition, deferring to our German language in which we were born, we have put double w as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation at the end, which, according to the Greek number, we have formed thus: [unclear]. We shall set down this script of the Nortmanni from the following order of Greek letters by imitation.

Quod &; literis Graecis fieri potest solitis ad votum et arbitrium in- dustriosi cuiusq́; scribentis. Doctißimus ille quondam praeceptor meus Ioan- nes Camerarius Dalburgius, Ecclesiae Vvormatiensis reuerendißimus antistes aliquot millia dictionũ Grae- carum collegerat, quae in viraque lingua Graeca et Germanica idem significant. Et Druidas priscos in Gallia Pontifices sacrorum Graeco sermone vsos fuis- se maximè in sacris, Caesar testatur in Commenta- rijs. Verum Romanis orbem deuastantibus, suarum vsum literarum tandem cum dominio multis natio- nibus violenter imposuerunt. Postremo reliquiae Troianorum qui postea dicti sunt Franci anno ante incarnationem Domini quadringentesimo quadra- gesimo de Scytharum finibus egreßi Marcomero re- ge praebente ducatum venerunt in Germaniam, &amp; à Saxonibus fratribus ad ostia Rheni sedes acceperunt. Qui deinceps per annos quinquaginta supranonin- gentos bellum cum Romanis et amp; Gallis pene conti- nuum agentes, vt Hunibaldus est author, totam po- stremo ferè Europam suo imperio seu regno subdi- derunt. Literas tamen Romanorum semel acceptat non extinxerunt, sed ipsi potiùs commixti inter Ger- manos et amp; Gallos didicerunt linguam eorum, &amp; ser- uauerunt literas eorum et amp; formam scripturarum. By the service of this alphabet the Normans wrote, in a secure communication, whatever they wished to keep hidden among themselves. No Greek could understand this method of writing, since, although all these characters are Greek, nevertheless they represent Latin letters according to numerical order; nor could it be understood by a Latin who had not first acquired knowledge of this art. This mode of writing can also be varied in many ways, when by transposition the numbers and the letters are changed. This can also be done with the usual Greek letters, at the wish and discretion of any industrious writer. Nor will the manner of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has been somewhat accustomed to it. The characters written above are also sufficiently suited to the German language; with them we can denote everything that occurs to us, in whatever speech we may be skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter k, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above.

On the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks

The opinion of many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they also steadfastly affirm that they used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. For they say that great consonance exists between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned former teacher of mine, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, the most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in the Commentaries that the ancient Druids in Gaul, the priests of sacred rites, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But as the Romans devastated the world, they at last violently imposed, together with their dominion, the use of their letters upon many nations.

Finally, the remnants of the Trojans, who afterward were called Franks, in the four hundred and fortieth year before the incarnation of the Lord, having gone out from the territories of the Scythians, with King Marcomer providing leadership, came into Germany and received settlements at the mouths of the Rhine from their brothers the Saxons. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years they waged an almost continuous war with the Romans and the Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, and at last subjected almost all Europe to their empire or kingdom. Yet they did not abolish the letters of the Romans once they had accepted them; rather, mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they themselves learned their language, and preserved their letters and form of writing.

The writer of the histories of this people, Wastbald, wrote in his native tongue books of the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes through almost seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the characters appended, as Hunibald says, which he mentions in his volume that he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Λ Ε ρ n Θ ε ζι β Ο χ Χ Λ Υ λ γ ι Ι ο Ρ φ Δ δ h K E P ψ σ δ e λ + P Γ α π ε 3 H m C F Ω ∞

Unless an error of the scribe has deceived me, I have suitably represented, as I think, Wastbald’s alphabet, in which some characters differ entirely from Greek ones, and several also seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what to judge: whoever their inventor was, he nevertheless observed the form of the Greek letters. The codex, decayed by excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have rather been deceived by some interpolator than found the true and certain opinion of Hunibald. But let us pass on to what remains, since if Hunibald’s statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is someone’s fiction, it will neither harm us nor do injury to the reader. Another fictitious alphabet follows, found in the codex of Hunibald, to which this was inscribed:

From the Grammatical Writings of Otfrid, Monk of Weissenburg

We read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, attempted, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, to regulate the German language. And when, as Turpin bears witness, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being delayed by frequent incursions of wars, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; nor did another arise after him who would bring the care of this matter back to mind.

But the aforesaid Otfrid, a monk, formerly a hearer and disciple of Rabanus of Fulda, under Louis the Pious, son of that Charles, having acquired that grammar, though imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound forth the admirable weight of regular instruction. For he composed many poems according to that same standard, in heroic meter and also in elegiac, and in addition composed some works in prose, addressed to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also to Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others.

Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too extracted these present characters of the alphabet from many, lest they utterly perish. It is established, moreover, on Otfrid’s testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, which he might use securely, throughout his very broad kingdom, in secret matters with individual prefects. From these, with Otfrid supplying them, we entrust a few things to these letters.

ZI A P Z T N 7 t † B L H C O G V X K S m I U R Q Y T D F K L ß T ψ z C o e Λ m ψ s Ψ w

Charles the Great, most Christian king and emperor, waged war with the Saxons for no fewer than thirty years, whom at last, overcoming them by the sword, he converted to the Christian faith. But fearing that they would again apostatize from the faith, as they had done several times, he appointed certain secret investigators, to whom he granted judicial power, so that, traveling through all Saxony, they should secretly and diligently inquire concerning the faith and morals of the people; and whoever they found to have apostatized from the faith, robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, despisers of the Church and of its priests and commandments, or those disturbing the Christian commonwealth with notorious crimes, or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they should without delay, by imperial and royal authority, hang with a noose with impunity, or otherwise kill as they could.

And so that this institution might remain forever unshaken, he gave the same men power also to appoint others, suitable under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid faculty, should exercise with impunity the office of inquiry and of death against the guilty. Finally, he prescribed for them secret laws and hidden signs, together with a form of oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, being mutually known to one another, might remain hidden from others, and preserve forever the necessary, more secret judgment in Saxon land. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, all of which at length entirely fell out of use. Nevertheless the office of this sort of inquisition remains down to the present time; its ministers are commonly called Feimeri.

Although these characters do not appear sufficiently beautiful and elegant, nevertheless it pleased me to join them with the aforesaid new inventions of mine, because of honor and reverence for antiquity, since there is no one even a little diligent who could not devise more beautiful ones for himself according to his own judgment. Yet continued practice in writing will be able, with easy compensation, to correct this misshapen crookedness, and, when frequently brought into habit, to make it pleasing. For no one, however learned or skilled in any language, also becomes a good writer unless by long practice he has transformed use into art. Another follows.

Θ α ζ ψ h o ∞ i x p q k t v s z f A m φ d w

If anyone wishes to fashion a new alphabet for himself according to his own judgment, he should know that two things in particular must be observed, which nevertheless I do not always find preserved in the foregoing. The first is that he form characters easy to handle; and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he arrange the individual letters in such a way that, when joined into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. I add a third, not promised: if you want the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, in the manner of the Hebrews.

Pharamund too, king of the Franks in Germany after Marcomer, who had brought the people in, the forty-third, and he died in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 426, when he had sent his scouts through Gaul for the purpose of invasion, ordered them to write in such characters.

Besides that alphabet of the Northmen which we placed at the beginning of this sixth book, we have also found the following written out in Bede.

From Latin letters also multiple alphabets are made, when, either reduced to number according to the model which we handed down in the preceding fifth book, or otherwise, in imitation of the Northmen, together with Greek letters they provide a method even for our own letters, for communicating most securely whatever we wish. Let us consequently set down, according to the number and order of our usual alphabet, the letters themselves changed in an unusual way, and we shall have a secret and mystical method of writing, sufficiently fine and elegant, confirmed by usage. This method of numbering, however, is different from the one which we placed in the fifth book, and is more suited to our purpose.

You now have, from Latin letters, a foreign alphabet, such as, as we said above, the Northmen once made for themselves from Greek letters. With it, if the necessary care is observed, you will safely write to a friend who knows the invention whatever you wish for the occasion. Let us add also another, which we judge safer.

Although in Latin speech we have no need of k, y, and w, yet because we use k and w in German, we have carried this alphabet also down to the twenty-fourth number and extended it. This method of writing, too, can be varied in many ways at pleasure. [unclear] according to the will of every writer.

There follows another alphabet of Honorius, surnamed the Theban, by whose service he concealed his magical follies, as Peter of Abano testifies in his larger book, the fourth.

I have also found another alphabet, newly devised by a certain alchemist, which he was accustomed to use for concealing his secrets, making a great valuation of his art, which contains little in itself besides words. For alchemy is loved by many, and is chaste.

O A S E N X T Θ b Ω H M O I V θ C ω I U P Ξ X C d δ K U Q O Y ɔ e Φ L Ψ R W Z φ F ε m X S W

Alchemy has many household attendants, who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance and present themselves under her name, so that they may preserve her, untouched for all time, from intercourse with so many importunate lovers. Vanity, fraud, craftiness, deception, sophistry, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the handmaids of alchemy; pretending that their mistress is beloved, they keep her inviolate, and readily prostitute themselves to those moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers after her.

On the Notes and the Wondrous, but Excessively Laborious, Method of Writing of M. T. Cicero, and after him of St. Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of notes of no small size. St. Cyprian, bishop of the Carthaginians and martyr, enlarged it with many notes for words, adding terms necessary for the uses of Christians, so that the work itself became useful not only to pagans, but much more also to the faithful. The codex is rare; I have found it only once, and bought it for a low price. For when, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1496, I was examining several libraries out of love of books, I found the aforementioned codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected because of its great age, thrown under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, at how much he valued it. He answered that he would prefer to it the little works of St. Anselm recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter occurred in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested little works of Anselm for the sixth part of a florin, handed them over to the rejoicing abbot and monks, and rescued the codex, which was already close to perishing. For they had decided, out of love of the parchment, that it should be scraped. Almost two years after this, I went up on horseback to Strasbourg on affairs of my order and, being admitted by Johannes Keisersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the major church, I found an entire Psalter written out in the same notes of Tullius and Cyprian, and most elegantly written with golden chapter initials. But the title had been placed on the outside by someone ignorant of the mystery as follows: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I brought in a scholar, showed the falsity, and advised that it be rewritten thus: “Psalter written in Ciceronian notes.” Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, since I did not afterwards return to that library. So that you may see, reader, the form of Cicero's notation, we have determined to set down a few notes below.

Sed parcant mihi pre- corlectores, quippe quem volũtas quidem propria re- traxit ab his studiis puerilibus, ne dicam in partem sal- tem vanis, sed quorundam instantia vt ea scriberem me compulit amicorum, quibus id negare nec potui nec debui fine iniuria necessitudinis contractae. Quorum nihilominus precatione inductus, etiam capitulum sc- quens me oportuit praescriptis connectere, pro lite- ris numeros collocare. Varios enim atque multiplices scribendi modos, veteres ob numerorum figuras col- locarunt, quibus adinuentione subtili arcana sua tuto alterutrum transmiferunt. Precibus itaque amicum persuasi, paucos ex multis in fine huius libri sextimo- dos posuimus, quibus iter ad notitiam aliorum pateat nescientibus.Nam si quem ista scire delectat, facilè po- terit ab eis cognitis ad altiora confeendere, modo- inuentos multiplici vicissitudine pro suo arbitrio va- riare. This method of writing demands a great memory, and a wholly enormous labor of reading, where any given character signifies either a whole word, or the final syllable, or some part of speech suited to the composition of the whole. Therefore, omitting all the signs, let us draw an alphabet from a few.
